answer_text:
Let  
\[
g(z)=\frac{f(z)}{2}.
\]
Then \(g:\mathbb D\to\mathbb C\) is analytic and \(|g(z)|<1\) for all \(z\in\mathbb D\).

Write the Taylor expansion
\[
g(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n z^n.
\]
Since \(f''(0)=4i\),
\[
c_2=\frac{g''(0)}{2!}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{f''(0)}{2}
=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2i=i.
\]
Thus \(|c_2|=1\).

For \(0<r<1\), by Parseval’s identity on the circle \(|z|=r\),
\[
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} |g(re^{i\theta})|^2\,d\theta
=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} |c_n|^2 r^{2n}.
\]
Because \(|g|<1\), the left-hand side is \(<1\). Letting \(r\to1^-\) gives
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} |c_n|^2 \le 1.
\]
But \(|c_2|^2=1\), so all other coefficients must vanish:
\[
c_n=0 \quad \text{for } n\neq 2.
\]
Hence
\[
g(z)=i z^2,
\]
and therefore
\[
f(z)=2g(z)=2i z^2.
\]

Now evaluate at \(z=i/2\):
\[
f\!\left(\frac i2\right)=2i\left(\frac i2\right)^2
=2i\left(-\frac14\right)
=-\frac{i}{2}.
\]

\[
\boxed{-\frac{i}{2}}
\]
